gender.family: fine-tuned ViT-B/16 averaged with CLIP ViT-B/32 zero-shot

insights.label: Arrival rate
insights.text: 43 people in 40 seconds of footage - too short to say anything about an hourly rate.

insights.label: Peak window
insights.text: The busiest 5 seconds started at 0:10 with 5 arrivals, while the quietest stretches had none.

insights.label: Dwell
insights.text: 65% stayed more than 30 seconds and 5% passed straight through - the typical visit was 40 seconds.

insights.label: Composition
insights.text: 54% of visitors were men (95% interval 36-69%, n = 32 tracks), and the biggest age group was 16-30 (67%).

insights.label: Spatial concentration
insights.text: The center of the camera view drew 44% of visitors, who stayed 35 seconds on average.

insights.label: Longest-staying group
insights.text: Female visitors aged 16-30 stayed longest (39 seconds on average, 7 people).

guide.headline: About 34 people were in view at any moment, 38 at the busiest.

setting.label: People sat and stayed
setting.text: People mostly sat and stayed, as in a café, restaurant, classroom or waiting area, so seats and how long people stay matter more than how many walked past.

sections.title: How busy it was
sections.headline: About 34 people were in view at any moment, 38 at the busiest, around 16:53.
sections.explain: This counts people visible at the same time, like looking up and counting heads. It does not depend on telling people apart, so it is one of the more reliable numbers here.
do: The room stayed about as full all the time (34 on average, 38 at most), so steady staffing fits better than extra cover at one moment.

series.label: People in view through the recording

sections.why: Counting heads at one moment only needs the detector to see people, not to follow them.
sections.tip: About as full all the time: steady staffing fits.
sections.brief: Counts heads at one moment, so it does not need to tell people apart.

proof.caption: The busiest moment, with everyone counted

sections.title: When people arrived
sections.headline: 15 people arrived during the recording, and 28 were already there when it started.
sections.explain: An arrival is someone the system starts following. People already in view when the recording starts are not counted as arrivals, because they came in earlier.
do: Plan staff from 'How busy it was', which counts heads and does not depend on following people.
This recording is only 40 seconds long. Process a few full days, and the Trends tab will show which hours and weekdays are reliably busy.
sections.why: In a few minutes of a seated room, almost every new track is someone the tracker lost behind another person and found again, not someone walking in.
sections.tip: Plan from 'How busy it was' instead.
sections.brief: Too short to tell arrivals from people found again.

proof.caption: A track ended and a new one began in the same spot

sections.title: Did people stop?
sections.headline: Too short to tell: 35 of 43 people were already in view when the recording started or still there when it ended.
sections.explain: A stay is measured from first to last sighting. When the recording starts or stops in the middle of someone's visit, the real stay is longer than what was seen.
do: Record longer stretches, ideally whole opening hours, to see how long people really stay.
sections.why: Most stays here were cut off by the start or end of the recording.

stat.label: stays cut off by the recording

sections.sub: Too short to tell how long people stay
sections.brief: Most stays were cut off by the start or end of the recording.

sections.title: Where people went
sections.headline: Most people were on the middle of the view; the left side saw the fewest.
sections.explain: The view is split into three equal strips, left, middle and right, and each person is counted in the strip where they spent most of their time.
do: The middle of the view drew the most people (44%). Put best-sellers and anything you want noticed there.
The left side was quiet (21%). Better lighting, a sign, or moving a popular item there can pull people across.
The Floor tab shows exactly where people stood and walked, as a heat map you can replay.
sections.why: Based on where each tracked person was; the strips are parts of the picture, not of the floor.

stat.label: of people were in the middle

sections.tip: Put what you want noticed in the middle.
sections.brief: The strips are thirds of the picture, not of the floor.

proof.caption: Where people spent time, over the whole recording

sections.title: Who visited
sections.headline: Roughly 28% women and 72% men among the 32 people the system was sure about, and the largest age group 16-30 (94%).
sections.explain: Each person is judged on several pictures taken through their stay, and the guesses are pooled. When the guesses disagree or are unsure, the person is left as 'not sure'.
do: Use this as a rough guide to who visits, never to judge an individual.
The system said 'not sure' for 26% of people rather than guess. Cameras placed at head height, facing the door, give it much better views.
sections.why: Gender and age are guessed from small, low-resolution pictures, often from behind or above.

stat.label: men, of the 32 it was sure about

sections.tip: A rough guide to who visits; never use it to judge one person.
sections.brief: Guessed from small pictures, often from behind or above.

sections.title: How far to trust this
sections.headline: Some numbers here are solid, some are rough guides. Each section above says which.
sections.explain: Solid: counting people visible at one moment. Rough: anything that follows one person over time, or guesses who they are. Each section's note says why.
do: 40 seconds of footage is a snapshot; patterns need several days.
Nobody is identified: use this to understand the space, not to watch people.

glossary.means: How many people the camera sees at the same moment.
Someone the system starts following during the recording.
How long one person stayed in view, from first to last sighting.
Stayed at least 30 seconds: usually someone looking properly.
Someone was inside the area drawn for it.
Share of the recording a seat or table was taken.
How many separate stays a seat or table had per hour.
The stay began before the recording did, so it lasted at least that long.
The system's guesses disagreed or were weak, so it gave no answer instead of a wrong one.
How far a number can be trusted, and each section says why.
